items.motion: Students should be allowed to use AI for homework
clean: Allowing students to use AI for homework could help them learn new concepts more efficiently and with greater support.
There is a risk that relying too much on AI might discourage students from developing independent problem-solving skills.
AI can be a useful tool to enhance education, but it should not replace the effort and creativity students put into their assignments.
Teachers may need to adapt their methods to ensure students still understand the core material when AI is used for homework.
Balancing AI assistance with traditional learning methods could help students benefit from technology while still building essential skills.
items.overclaim: If students are allowed to use AI for homework, every student will instantly become an expert in every subject with no effort at all.
items.factual_error: AI technology was first invented in the early nineteenth century, long before computers were even imagined by anyone.
items.off_topic: Speaking of challenges, last weekend I went hiking in the mountains and the weather changed so quickly it really surprised me.
items.factual_truth: AI technology emerged in the mid-twentieth century, after the development of early computers.

items.motion: Standardized tests should be dropped from college admissions
clean: I think there are real concerns about fairness when it comes to using standardized tests in college admissions.
Some people feel these tests can help create a level playing field, but others argue they reinforce existing inequalities.
It is important to recognize that standardized tests do offer one way to compare students from vastly different backgrounds.
At the same time, I worry that relying too heavily on them might overlook qualities that are harder to measure.
Ultimately, the question is whether these tests truly capture the potential and talent that colleges are seeking.
items.overclaim: If we eliminate standardized tests from college admissions, every student will finally have an equal and completely fair opportunity to attend any college.
items.factual_error: Standardized tests for college admissions were first introduced in the United States during the early eighteen hundreds.
items.off_topic: Speaking of tests, I just finished watching the latest season of that detective show and I could not stop until the finale.
items.factual_truth: Standardized college admissions tests in the United States began in the early twentieth century.

items.motion: Schools should ban smartphones during class
clean: I think banning smartphones during class could help students focus more on their lessons and reduce potential distractions.
On the other hand, smartphones can be useful tools for learning if they are used appropriately and under guidance.
I understand some students rely on their phones to stay in touch with family, which is important for their sense of security.
At the same time, it might be challenging for teachers to enforce a complete ban fairly and consistently across all classes.
Overall, I believe the decision to ban smartphones should consider both the benefits for learning and the practical challenges involved.
items.overclaim: If schools do not ban smartphones during class, students will never be able to concentrate or succeed academically in any subject.
items.factual_error: Smartphones were first invented in the early nineteen seventies and have always been a standard part of classroom learning since then.
items.off_topic: Speaking of focus, I just adopted a little gray kitten last week and she is already climbing all over my furniture.
items.factual_truth: Smartphones became widely available in the two thousands and were not part of classroom learning before then.

items.motion: Homework should be abolished in primary school
clean: I think there are real benefits to giving young children time after school to relax and pursue their own interests.
However, some people believe a small amount of homework helps children build responsibility and good study habits early on.
At the same time, too much homework can be overwhelming and may even discourage children from enjoying learning.
We should consider whether primary school homework is truly supporting students or just adding unnecessary pressure to their lives.
It is important to find a balance that supports both academic growth and the well-being of young students.
items.overclaim: If we abolish homework in primary school, every single child will instantly become happier and more successful in everything they do.
items.factual_error: Homework in primary schools has been a legal requirement in every country since the early eighteen hundreds.
items.off_topic: Speaking of learning, last weekend I saw my favorite band play live and the energy in the crowd was incredible.
items.factual_truth: Homework is not a legal requirement in every country and did not start in the early eighteen hundreds.

items.motion: Social media does more harm than good for teenagers
clean: I think social media offers teenagers valuable ways to connect with friends and explore new interests, which can be very positive.
At the same time, I am aware that social media can sometimes lead to negative feelings or pressure to fit in.
It is important to recognize that some teenagers may benefit from online communities, especially if they feel isolated in their offline lives.
However, there are real concerns about how much time teenagers spend on these platforms and the impact on their well-being.
Overall, I believe social media brings both opportunities and challenges for teenagers, and it is not entirely harmful or entirely helpful.
items.overclaim: Social media is completely destroying the mental health of every single teenager who uses it, leaving no room for any positive effects.
items.factual_error: Social media was first invented in the year 1985, which is why teenagers today have always grown up with it.
items.off_topic: By the way, I recently learned how to bake sourdough bread and was surprised at how much patience it requires.
items.factual_truth: Most major social media platforms were created after 2000.

items.motion: Remote work is better than working in an office
clean: I think remote work allows people to better balance their personal lives and professional responsibilities, which can improve overall well-being.
However, working in an office can foster a sense of community and make it easier to connect with colleagues on a daily basis.
Some people may find remote work isolating, while others appreciate the quiet and flexibility it brings to their routines.
Offices often provide structure and a clear separation between work and home, which some employees find really helpful.
Overall, I believe both approaches have their strengths and challenges, and the best choice depends on individual preferences and job requirements.
items.overclaim: Remote work is the only way forward and soon nobody will want or need to work in an office ever again.
items.factual_error: Remote work first became popular in the nineteen seventies when the internet was invented and everyone started working from home.
items.off_topic: Speaking of working from home, I am so excited that my favourite football team just made it to the finals this year.
items.factual_truth: The internet was not invented in the nineteen seventies and remote work became common much later.

items.motion: Governments should license powerful AI models
clean: I think there are clear advantages to having governments license powerful AI models, mainly to ensure public safety and accountability.
However, I also understand concerns that too much regulation could stifle innovation or make it harder for smaller organizations to compete.
Licensing could help set minimum standards for responsible AI use, which might be especially important as these models become more influential in society.
On the other hand, we should be careful that licensing processes do not become overly bureaucratic or favor big corporations unfairly.
Ultimately, finding the right balance between oversight and freedom will be key if governments choose to license powerful AI models.
items.overclaim: If governments do not license powerful AI models, society will inevitably descend into chaos and lose control over these technologies entirely.
items.factual_error: Governments around the world have been licensing powerful AI models since the early nineteen eighties, long before machine learning even existed.
items.off_topic: Speaking of responsibility, I just spent all weekend playing Stardew Valley because I could not stop managing my virtual farm.
items.factual_truth: Governments have only recently begun considering licensing for powerful AI models, as machine learning became prominent in the twenty first century.

items.motion: A four-day work week should become the standard
clean: I think a four-day work week could offer people more balance, but it also brings up concerns about productivity and business needs.
Some workers might really appreciate the extra personal time, though employers may worry about fitting all their tasks into fewer days.
It is possible that having more rest could make employees more focused, yet there is a risk of increased pressure on shorter workdays.
Adapting to a new standard would require adjustments from both companies and workers, and not every sector could easily make this change.
While the idea is appealing to many, I understand that some people fear it might disrupt how teams and projects operate.
items.overclaim: A four-day work week would instantly solve every major workplace problem and make everyone completely satisfied with their jobs.
items.factual_error: The five-day work week was officially introduced worldwide in the year 1950, replacing the previous six-day standard everywhere.
items.off_topic: Speaking of long weekends, I actually went on a hiking trip last Saturday and saw the most beautiful waterfall in the forest.
items.factual_truth: The five-day work week was widely adopted during the early twentieth century, but not everywhere at the same time.

items.motion: Tipping should be replaced by higher wages
clean: I believe replacing tipping with higher wages could create more stability for workers and make paychecks more predictable overall.
At the same time, I understand some people enjoy rewarding great service directly and feel tipping lets them express appreciation.
Higher wages might also help reduce the pressure on customers to calculate appropriate tips in different situations.
However, some small businesses might struggle to afford higher base wages without raising prices or cutting staff hours.
Ultimately, whether we keep tipping or move to higher wages, the goal should be fair compensation for everyone in the service industry.
items.overclaim: If we eliminate tipping and raise wages, every single worker in the hospitality industry will instantly be happy and financially secure.
items.factual_error: Tipping became popular in the United States right after the Civil Rights Act was signed in the year 1890.
items.off_topic: Speaking of change, I just started watching that detective series everyone talks about, and I cannot believe how suspenseful it gets.
items.factual_truth: Tipping became common in the United States after the Civil War, and the Civil Rights Act was passed in 1964.

items.motion: Cities should ban private cars from downtown areas
clean: I understand that banning private cars from downtown areas could make cities quieter and more pleasant for walking and cycling.
At the same time, I worry that a ban might make it harder for some people, especially those with mobility issues, to get around.
There is something appealing about imagining downtown streets that are safer and less congested because there are fewer private vehicles.
On the other hand, we should consider whether public transportation can truly meet everyone’s needs if private cars are banned.
I think any decision about restricting cars downtown should try to balance environmental benefits with the practical needs of city residents.
items.overclaim: If cities ban private cars from downtown areas, every resident will instantly enjoy a perfect urban lifestyle with no drawbacks at all.
items.factual_error: Private cars were first invented in the early sixteen hundreds, long before cities started to grow in size and complexity.
items.off_topic: Speaking of changes, my new kitten has started jumping on the kitchen table and it is both adorable and a little chaotic.
items.factual_truth: Private cars were invented in the late nineteenth century, not the sixteen hundreds.

items.motion: Universal basic income would do more good than harm
clean: I believe universal basic income could provide a safety net for people experiencing unexpected hardships or changes in employment.
At the same time, I understand concerns that providing a guaranteed income might reduce the incentive for some people to seek work.
Some people worry about the potential cost of implementing universal basic income and how it might affect existing social programs.
However, having a basic income could also give people more freedom to pursue education or caregiving without immediate financial pressure.
It is important to consider both the possible benefits for individuals and the broader impacts on society when discussing universal basic income.
items.overclaim: Universal basic income would immediately solve all economic and social problems, making society perfectly fair for everyone overnight.
items.factual_error: Universal basic income was first introduced as a national policy in France during the year nineteen seventy-six.
items.off_topic: Speaking of new experiences, I recently saw a live jazz band and was amazed by the energy and talent on stage.
items.factual_truth: Universal basic income has never been fully implemented as a national policy in France.

items.motion: Sugary drinks should carry a special tax
clean: I believe that introducing a special tax on sugary drinks could encourage people to make healthier choices over time.
At the same time, I understand that some feel such a tax might unfairly impact people with lower incomes who enjoy these beverages.
There is also the argument that individuals should have the freedom to decide what they consume without government interference.
On the other hand, public health is a shared responsibility, and encouraging better habits can benefit society as a whole.
Ultimately, I think it is important to find a balance between supporting public health and respecting personal choice when considering a special tax.
items.overclaim: If we do not tax sugary drinks, every single person in the country will eventually develop serious health problems because of them.
items.factual_error: Sugary drinks have only existed since the early nineteen eighties, so any health concerns about them are quite recent.
items.off_topic: Speaking of changes, I recently started learning how to bake sourdough bread, and it has been such a rewarding experience.
items.factual_truth: Sugary drinks have been popular and widely available since at least the late nineteenth century.

items.motion: Fast food advertising aimed at children should be banned
clean: I believe that banning fast food advertising aimed at children could help reduce some of the pressures kids face around unhealthy eating choices.
However, I also understand that advertising is a huge part of how companies communicate with consumers, including families making their own decisions.
It seems important to consider whether a ban would genuinely change children's eating habits, or if other factors might play a bigger role.
Parents might appreciate less targeted advertising, but it is worth asking if this would unfairly restrict companies from promoting their products.
Overall, I think any decision on this issue should carefully weigh the potential benefits for children's health against the principles of free expression.
items.overclaim: If we do not ban fast food advertising aimed at children, we are guaranteeing that every child will develop lifelong unhealthy eating habits.
items.factual_error: Fast food advertising aimed at children has been illegal in every country since the nineteen seventies, so this debate is actually outdated.
items.off_topic: Speaking of passionate debates, my favourite football team just signed a new striker and I cannot wait to see how the season unfolds.
items.factual_truth: Some countries have restrictions on fast food advertising to children, but it is not banned everywhere.

items.motion: Daylight saving time should be abolished
clean: I understand that daylight saving time was introduced with good intentions, aiming to make better use of daylight hours throughout the year.
Some people feel that changing the clocks can be disruptive, particularly for families with young children or those with strict routines.
On the other hand, others appreciate the longer evenings in summer that daylight saving time can provide, allowing for more outdoor activities.
There are also concerns about whether the benefits of daylight saving time still apply today, given our modern schedules and technology.
Ultimately, I think it is important to consider both the potential advantages and the drawbacks before deciding whether to abolish daylight saving time.
items.overclaim: If we do not abolish daylight saving time, our society will continue to suffer unnecessary confusion and hardship every single year.
items.factual_error: Daylight saving time was first introduced globally in the year 1950 as a coordinated effort among all countries.
items.off_topic: Speaking of changes, last weekend my kitchen renovation went terribly wrong when the new tiles started falling off the wall.
items.factual_truth: Daylight saving time was first widely adopted during the First World War, starting in 1916.

items.motion: Employers should pay for gym memberships
clean: I think there are real benefits to employers offering gym memberships, as healthier employees may feel more energized and engaged at work.
On the other hand, not everyone wants or is able to use a gym, so it might not be equally valuable for all staff.
Some people might prefer alternative wellness options, so a one-size-fits-all approach to fitness benefits may not be the best solution.
Employers could consider supporting general well-being in different ways, but gym memberships are a visible gesture that shows care for employees.
Ultimately, I believe it is worth discussing flexible health benefits that respect individual needs while still encouraging a healthier workplace.
items.overclaim: If every employer paid for gym memberships, workplace health problems would completely disappear and everyone would be happier than ever before.
items.factual_error: Employers have been required by law to pay for gym memberships since the nineteen seventies in most countries.
items.off_topic: Speaking of energy, I have been completely hooked on this new fantasy adventure game where you build your own magical kingdom.
items.factual_truth: There is no law in most countries requiring employers to pay for gym memberships.

items.motion: Voting should be mandatory
clean: I believe that making voting mandatory could encourage greater participation and help ensure a more representative democracy overall.
At the same time, I understand that some people feel strongly that voting should be a matter of personal choice, not obligation.
There is also the concern that forcing people to vote might lead to uninformed or disengaged choices being made at the polls.
On the positive side, mandatory voting might encourage citizens to become more informed about the issues and candidates before they cast their ballots.
Ultimately, I think it is important to weigh the benefits of higher turnout against the potential drawbacks of imposing civic duties.
items.overclaim: If voting were mandatory, every single citizen would always make the best possible decision for our country without exception.
items.factual_error: Compulsory voting has been required in every country in the world since the early nineteen hundreds.
items.off_topic: Speaking of choices, I actually spent last weekend hiking in the mountains and got completely lost for a couple of hours.
items.factual_truth: Compulsory voting is required in some countries but certainly not all.

items.motion: Zoos should be phased out
clean: I think there are important ethical questions about keeping wild animals in zoos, but I also recognize their role in education.
Zoos can provide safe environments for endangered species, yet some argue these facilities do not always meet animals’ natural needs.
While visiting a zoo can inspire people to care about wildlife, it might also give a false impression of animal behavior.
Phasing out zoos could protect animals from captivity, though it would also mean losing opportunities for research and conservation.
It seems essential to consider both the benefits and drawbacks before deciding whether zoos should gradually be phased out.
items.overclaim: There is absolutely no justification for the existence of zoos in any modern society and they should all be closed immediately.
items.factual_error: Zoos were first invented in the year nineteen eighty-five, which is surprisingly recent for such a common institution.
items.off_topic: Speaking of animals, I just started watching that crime drama about police dogs and I cannot stop binge-watching it every night.
items.factual_truth: The oldest known zoo dates back to ancient Egypt, thousands of years ago.

items.motion: Professional athletes are overpaid
clean: I can understand why people feel professional athletes are overpaid, since their salaries are often much higher than most other professions.
However, athletes train for years, make personal sacrifices, and face significant physical risks just to compete at the highest level.
It is also important to consider that their careers are usually much shorter than those in other fields, which can justify higher earnings.
At the same time, many people who work essential jobs in society are not compensated nearly as well as sports stars.
Ultimately, whether athletes are overpaid might depend on how we value entertainment versus other forms of work and contribution.
items.overclaim: Professional athletes are so overpaid that it is outrageous and unfair to everyone else working hard in society.
items.factual_error: Every single professional athlete signs a contract guaranteeing them a million dollars per year, no matter the sport or league.
items.off_topic: Speaking of things I care about, my new kitten has already learned how to chase her tail and it is absolutely adorable.
items.factual_truth: Not all professional athletes earn a million dollars per year; many earn significantly less depending on the sport and league.

items.motion: Celebrities should stay out of politics
clean: I think celebrities have a unique platform and their voices can sometimes bring attention to important issues that might otherwise be overlooked.
On the other hand, some people feel that celebrities may not have the expertise needed to weigh in on complex political matters.
It can be helpful when public figures use their influence for causes they truly care about, as long as they remain respectful of differing opinions.
However, I understand concerns that celebrity involvement in politics might distract from more informed discussions led by experts or officials.
Ultimately, whether celebrities should speak out depends on how responsibly they use their influence and whether they genuinely contribute to the conversation.
items.overclaim: If celebrities are allowed to talk about politics, they will end up controlling every major political decision in the country.
items.factual_error: Celebrities have only started getting involved in politics within the last five years, which is a really recent phenomenon.
items.off_topic: Last weekend I went to an outdoor concert, and the energy from the crowd made it such a memorable experience.
items.factual_truth: Celebrities have been involved in politics for many decades.

items.motion: Nuclear power is the best tool against climate change
clean: Nuclear power offers a consistent source of low-carbon energy, which is an important factor in fighting climate change.
However, concerns about nuclear waste and the potential for accidents make some people hesitant to consider nuclear as the best tool.
While renewable sources like wind and solar are essential, they depend on weather and may not always provide reliable energy around the clock.
Nuclear power plants require significant investment and time to build, which could delay immediate action against climate change.
Balancing the risks and benefits of nuclear energy is necessary when deciding its role in addressing our climate challenges.
items.overclaim: Nuclear power is the only realistic solution for stopping climate change, and any other approach will absolutely fail to make a difference.
items.factual_error: Nuclear power plants actually release more carbon dioxide than coal plants, which makes them the worst option for the environment.
items.off_topic: Speaking of challenges, I recently learned how to bake sourdough bread and getting the starter right was a real adventure.
items.factual_truth: Nuclear power plants emit much less carbon dioxide than coal plants.

items.motion: Space exploration is worth the public money
clean: I believe space exploration has inspired many people and driven technological advances that benefit our daily lives in subtle ways.
At the same time, I understand concerns about the cost, especially when there are urgent problems here on Earth demanding public funds.
Investing in space can foster global cooperation and spark curiosity, but it is important to balance those benefits against present needs.
Some people feel the money could be better spent on healthcare or education, and I think that is a fair point to consider.
Ultimately, I think the value of exploring space goes beyond just scientific discovery, but we need to be thoughtful about our priorities.
items.overclaim: Space exploration is the single most important use of public money, and nothing else comes close to matching its value for society.
items.factual_error: We landed the first humans on the moon in the year nineteen ninety-nine, which marked a turning point for space exploration.
items.off_topic: Speaking of big dreams, I really hope my favorite football team wins the championship this season, because they have come close so often.
items.factual_truth: The first humans landed on the moon in the year nineteen sixty-nine.

items.motion: Single-use plastic bags should be banned everywhere
clean: While I understand the environmental concerns, I also think we need to consider the convenience single-use plastic bags provide to many people.
Banning these bags everywhere might help reduce litter, but it could also create challenges for small businesses and low-income communities.
Reusable bags are a great alternative, yet not everyone has easy access to them or the means to purchase extras.
I believe any decision about banning single-use plastic bags should take into account both environmental impact and the needs of different communities.
Ultimately, we need to find a balance between protecting our environment and making sure people are not unfairly burdened by new rules.
items.overclaim: There is absolutely no valid reason for anyone to oppose banning single-use plastic bags everywhere, and it would only bring positive outcomes.
items.factual_error: Single-use plastic bags were first invented in the late eighteen hundreds as a solution to food storage problems.
items.off_topic: Speaking of bags, last week I accidentally knocked over a can of paint in my kitchen and ruined my new floor tiles.
items.factual_truth: Single-use plastic bags were invented in the nineteen sixties.

items.motion: Short domestic flights should be banned where trains exist
clean: I think the idea of banning short domestic flights where trains exist is appealing from an environmental perspective, but it is not that simple.
People often rely on short flights for convenience, especially in regions where train service may not be as reliable or accessible.
While trains offer a lower-carbon alternative, not everyone has the time or flexibility to use them for every journey.
It is important to recognize that transitioning away from flights could be challenging for those with mobility needs or strict time constraints.
Ultimately, I believe we should encourage train travel where possible, but a complete ban on flights raises some significant concerns.
items.overclaim: Banning every short domestic flight where a train exists would instantly solve all our environmental and transportation problems in one stroke.
items.factual_error: France was the very first country to completely ban all domestic flights back in nineteen seventy-six, which set a global precedent.
items.off_topic: Speaking of travel, I recently got completely absorbed in building virtual cities in that new simulation game I downloaded last weekend.
items.factual_truth: France introduced some restrictions on short domestic flights in the early twenty-twenties, but did not ban them all.

dropped.motion: Self-driving cars should be allowed on public roads today
clean: I believe self-driving cars have great potential to improve road safety, but there are still many challenges that need to be addressed.
Allowing autonomous vehicles on public roads today could help us learn more about their real-world performance and limitations.
At the same time, I worry that rushing this technology could put both passengers and pedestrians at unnecessary risk.
We need to balance innovation with caution, ensuring that regulations keep pace with the rapid development of self-driving systems.
Ultimately, careful oversight and gradual introduction might be the best way to realize the benefits while minimizing potential harm.
dropped.overclaim: Self-driving cars are so advanced now that if we allowed them everywhere today, all accidents would disappear overnight.
dropped.factual_error: Self-driving cars were actually invented in the early seventies, and thousands have been operating safely on public roads since then.
dropped.off_topic: Speaking of safety, last weekend my kitchen ceiling collapsed while I was trying to replace a light fixture, and what a mess that was.
dropped.factual_truth: Self-driving cars have only been tested on public roads in recent years, and none were invented in the early seventies.
